title: English Matters: An English Teacher Looks Back, Looks Within, Looks Ahead January 11, 2024
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
source: Dave Stuart Jr. (davestuartjr.com) — guest post by Jim Burke, retired 35-year English teacher,
summary: In this guest essay, retired 35-year English teacher Jim Burke traces his career from a barely-graduated high schooler through a Peace Corps stint teaching woodshop in Tunisia, into the classroom, and back out again at retirement, using his own trajectory to wrestle with the perennial question the 1987 English Coalition Conference posed but never resolved: what is English, and what are English teachers for? He recounts navigating decades of contested curriculum politics — from Common Core to #DisruptTexts to book-banning — while serving on standards committees with the conviction that it's "better to be at the table than on the menu." Anchoring the piece are two teacher-mentor stories: his own mentor Bev Edwards refusing to let a single book represent Black culture in a racially fraught community, and Mike Rose's teacher Mr. MacFarland's one-line affirmation, "Listen, you can write," which changed the course of Rose's life. Burke closes with a recent letter from a former student thanking him for teaching her resilience, using it as proof of his central claim: that English, done well, is "a discipline of hope."
points: Burke frames nearly four decades of curriculum battles (Common Core, #DisruptTexts, book bans) as evidence that English teachers have shifted from waiting to be told what to teach toward actively defining their own roles and responsibilities.

His mentor Bev Edwards's 1988 refusal to teach I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings as the department's sole representation of Black culture is offered as an early formative lesson that English teachers can say "no" to curricular consensus on principled grounds.

Burke's guiding philosophy for serving on standards and testing committees he sometimes disagreed with — "better to be at the table than on the menu" — models a specific stance toward institutional participation that resists both compliance and disengagement.

A single line from a mentor teacher ("Listen, you can write," said to a first-generation college student) is used to argue that English teachers' highest-leverage moments are often small and quiet rather than curricular grand gestures.
quotes: In 1987, sixty leaders in the field of English assembled at the English Coalition Conference (ECC) to discuss what "English" is and what it is, exactly, that English teachers do.

For me and those who have influenced me most, English has always been a discipline of hope, one which, at its best, teaches us to understand and to tell a better story about ourselves, each other, and our country.

In the last twenty years, English teachers have experienced a series of efforts to codify what we should teach; these mandates and initiatives came from institutions and organizations such as the National Board for Professional Teaching Standards, the College Board, Common Core Standards, as well as state and district agencies.

Yet my own belief regarding such opportunities has always been that it is better to be at the table than on the menu, as the saying goes. In other words, I always joined in good faith and with the hope that I could make a contribution that served our discipline, our profession, and our students.

Mr. MacFarland told Mike Rose in his senior year of high school, "Listen, you can write." It is in such small ways, such quiet moments that happen in class, through a comment in the margin on a student's paper, or during the sort of mentoring chats that arise after class that we highlight ours as a discipline of hope.

When I retired in June 2022, I had a series of exit interviews required by district protocols. They all asked me pretty much the same questions: What did I understand my job to be as an English teacher and how had it changed over the years since I began?
My answer: Yes. Yes. Yes. Absolutely. I cannot imagine having done anything else with my life.

I wanted to reach out because the program I'm in has been talking a lot about the importance of expressing gratitude for the mentors/people who have impacted your life/academic trajectory. You were the first teacher that ever made me feel anything positive about my writing and gave me confidence in myself.
